description: Creating a healthcare monitoring software for astronauts.
summary:
OrbitMSK is an aerospace-inspired web dashboard we built to help track astronaut muscle health and physical performance across preflight, in-flight, and postflight mission phases. In microgravity, astronauts lose strength and bone density quickly, which makes staying on top of daily exercise countermeasures like resistance training and treadmill sessions absolutely critical.

Our app brings all of those moving parts together into one clean control panel. It connects individual preflight baseline tests, daily workout records across equipment like ARED, Treadmill, CEVIS, and ROCKY, and wearable sensor readings from IMUs, force plates, and pressure insoles. Under the hood, a smart, rule-based engine automatically compares incoming performance data against the astronaut's personal baseline, calculates workout adherence, and flags any unusual drops so flight surgeons can take action early.

This project matters because keeping astronauts strong and mission-ready is essential for safe spacewalks and planetary landings. By combining offline-ready local storage, transparent math-based insights, and strict safety guardrails, OrbitMSK offers a reliable decision-support tool that bridges space exploration and remote terrestrial rehabilitation.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

OrbitMSK is an aerospace-inspired monitoring dashboard we built to help track astronaut musculoskeletal health and physical performance across preflight, in-flight, and postflight mission phases. In microgravity, astronauts lose muscle strength and bone density quickly, so NASA relies heavily on daily exercise countermeasures like resistance training and aerobic workouts. Our software brings all of those moving pieces into one place connecting individual preflight baseline tests, daily workout records across equipment like ARED, Treadmill, CEVIS, and ROCKY, and wearable sensor readings from IMUs, force sensors, and pressure insoles. Under the hood, a React frontend talks to a lightweight Node.js and Express backend that saves everything locally in structured JSON files. Whenever new performance or exercise data is logged, a built-in rule-based engine compares it against the astronaut's personal baseline, calculates adherence and percentage shifts, and flags anything that needs attention.

What benefits does it have?

Right now, exercise logs, sensor readings, and baseline assessments often live in separate places, making it harder to spot gradual changes during a long mission. OrbitMSK puts everything onto a single screen so flight surgeons, trainers, and crew members can see daily adherence trends and performance shifts at a glance. Because it runs completely locally without needing a cloud database or live internet connection, it is fast, reliable, and built with deep-space communication delays in mind. Just as importantly, its alerts are based on transparent, explainable math rather than a "black-box" AI, so specialists can immediately see which metric dropped and by how much.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Our goal is to help keep astronauts strong, safe, and mission-ready during long-duration spaceflight, especially when preparing for demanding spacewalks or returning to gravity. Beyond space exploration, the exact same approach applies directly here on Earth. The way OrbitMSK tracks personal baselines, movement consistency, and recovery trends can easily support remote physical therapy, injury rehabilitation, and high-performance athletic training where catching small declines early makes a huge difference.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

We built the entire prototype using JavaScript across the stack. For the frontend interface, we used React 18, Vite, React Router, Tailwind CSS, Recharts for the interactive performance graphs, Lucide React for icons, and Axios for API communication. On the backend, we used Node.js and Express with Helmet, CORS, and Morgan, storing all records locally via Node’s file system module with atomic writes so files never get corrupted. No specialized physical hardware was required for this software prototype all IMU, force, and pressure readings are handled through clean manual entry forms and clearly labeled simulated datasets.

How is your project creative?

Instead of building a generic spreadsheet or clinical form, we designed OrbitMSK to feel like a real mission-control telemetry console complete with a dark aerospace theme, mission-phase filters in the top bar, and instant baseline comparisons. One of the most thoughtful parts of our design is how strictly we handle data honesty and safety. Every record in the system is tagged by where it came from whether it is simulated demo data, a manual entry, or a rule-based calculation and we built clear guardrails into the interface reminding users that wearable sensors measure physical performance, not direct bone density or clinical diagnoses.

What factors did your team consider?

Scientific accuracy and safety boundaries were our top priorities. Wearable sensors like IMUs and force plates cannot directly diagnose muscle atrophy or osteoporosis, so we intentionally focused the software on measurable functional indicators like force production, joint range of motion, and movement velocity to support specialists rather than replace them. We also thought carefully about offline reliability and data integrity, building per-collection write queues on the backend so rapid updates never overwrite each other, and structuring the codebase cleanly so real hardware adapters or advanced AI models can be plugged in later without rebuilding the app.
